title: Transit fare strategy approved with lower fare caps
subtitle: Longer transfer times, advisory committee appointments and recruitment pause, master plans, and support for Bill 5 on councillor conduct.
overview: Council approved the Transit Fare Strategy with two changes to staff's plan. Kids aged 12 and under will ride free permanently. The fare capping loyalty program was approved with a gentler phase-in: the monthly cap starts at 32 rides and rises to 34 by 2026. Council also extended the fare transfer time to 90 minutes. Councillors said the changes ease the impact of the first fare increase since 2016 on loyal pass holders. Council will return to the 2024 to 2027 costs in the multi-year budget.

Council also approved the Water and Wastewater Servicing Master Plan and the Stormwater Management Master Plan, which went through on the consent report. It updated the Delegation of Authority By-law. It made appointments to several advisory committees and boards, and paused further advisory committee recruitment until a new governance framework is approved in late 2023, except where needed for quorum. The appointments followed a closed session on personal matters.
Council backed the Association of Municipalities of Ontario's call for stronger municipal codes of conduct and supported Bill 5, which deals with harassment and abuse by local leaders {{vote:m20}}.

decisions.detail: Council made the Kids Ride Free program for children aged 12 and under permanent, with budget impacts going to the 2024-2027 multi-year budget {{vote:m11}}.
Council approved fare capping with a monthly cap of 32 rides in 2023-2024, 33 in 2025 and 34 in 2026, with the 2023 cost of $19,900 managed through operating variance {{vote:m16}}.
Staff were given authority to proceed with the other fare strategy initiatives, and the permitted transfer time was extended to 90 minutes at an estimated $10,000 in 2023 {{vote:m18}}.

decisions.item: Water and Wastewater Servicing Master Plan
decisions.detail: Council approved the plan, directed staff to file the environmental assessment notice, and referred its financial information to the rate models and multi-year budget {{vote:m5}}.
Council approved the plan and referred its financial implications to the multi-year budget process {{vote:m6}}.
Recruitment and appointments to advisory committees are paused until the governance framework is approved in Q4 2023, except where needed to keep a quorum {{vote:m9}}.
Council appointed members to the Committee of Adjustment, Museums, Planning, Tourism and Water Conservation advisory committees and The Elliott Community Board of Trustees {{vote:m8}}.

decisions.item: Support for Bill 5 and code of conduct reform
decisions.detail: Council supported the Association of Municipalities of Ontario's call for stronger codes of conduct and backed Bill 5 on harassment and abuse by local leaders {{vote:m20}}.

debate: Delegates from a student association, a transit advocacy group and a resident broadly supported fare capping. Some opposed the size of the monthly pass increase, with one preferring to leave fares alone and another asking for the rise to be spread over two or three years.
A delegate argued that service quality, such as indirect routes and low frequency, matters more than fare design. A delegate also warned that fare increases usually cut ridership for a time.

Staff defended the plan as a balance that catches up after no fare increase since 2016, and said an affordable bus pass program remains available. They said about 18% of customers would be affected by the higher monthly pass price. One councillor argued for a slower phase-in for pass holders, and another proposal for a slower phase-in was defeated {{vote:m14}} because staff had not costed it.

On transfer times, supporters pointed to accessibility, missed connections and consistency with the transit master plan. Staff said engagement had not raised transfer times as a concern and that few trips fell between 60 and 90 minutes.

On Bill 5, one councillor asked who would define egregious conduct and raised concern about receiving the material late. The mover said the integrity commissioner and then a court would decide, and that the motion supports the bill's principles.
